identity.title: Instant Policy: In-Context Imitation Learning via Graph Diffusion

problem.claim: The paper addresses in-context imitation learning for robotics, where a robot learns new tasks from demonstrations.

contributions.claim: Instant Policy models in-context imitation learning as graph generation with a learned diffusion process over demonstrations, observations, and actions.
It proposes training with pseudo-demonstrations: arbitrary simulated trajectories intended to provide a virtually infinite training pool.
It presents the model as a foundation for cross-embodiment and zero-shot transfer to language-defined tasks.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish Instant Policy through two components: graph-diffusion modeling for structured reasoning and pseudo-demonstration training from simulation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report experiments in simulation and reality showing rapid learning of various everyday robot tasks.
The authors report cross-embodiment and zero-shot transfer to language-defined tasks.

narrative_sequence.summary: In-context learning motivates in-context imitation learning as an opportunity for robotics.
Instant Policy is introduced to learn new tasks from one or two demonstrations using two components.
The first component uses graph representations and learned diffusion to structure reasoning over demonstrations, observations, and actions.
The second component trains on arbitrary simulated trajectories as pseudo-demonstrations.
The authors report rapid learning in simulation and reality, plus cross-embodiment and language-defined zero-shot transfer.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs a structured representation for demonstrations with a training-data strategy based on simulated pseudo-demonstrations.

lessons.interpretation: A learning system can be framed by jointly specifying the representation that organizes context and how scalable context examples are generated.
lessons.application: When presenting a demonstration-driven method, state both the inductive structure used to interpret demonstrations and a concrete source of scalable training trajectories.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when simulated trajectories do not reflect the target environment or when the task lacks useful relational structure.

unknowns: The abstract gives no quantitative results, baselines, task inventory, or details about the one- or two-demonstration setting.
It does not specify how pseudo-demonstrations are generated, how closely simulation matches reality, or what cross-embodiment and zero-shot transfer conditions were tested.
